Done — committed and pushed (`167c0e7`). The repo now reads like a shipped project rather than one under construction:

**The root** is minimal: `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and the code. The README's command table now lists every shipped command including `ask`, `blame --why`, `review`, `sync`, and `doctor`.

**`architecture/`** holds only living documents — the four binding specs (`ARCHITECTURE.md`, now marked *Implemented* with its two recorded deviations; `DATA_MODEL.md`; `CLI_REFERENCE.md`; `REVIEW_UI.md` with a shipped-status banner) plus the new **`ROADMAP.md`**. Everything else — both executed build plans, MONOREPO_PLAN, the six original idea docs, the prior-art research, and all session handoffs — is archived under `architecture/history/` with links repaired, clearly labeled as "useful for archaeology, not needed for new work."

**The roadmap** is four tiers: (1) *hardening* — npm publish, the never-worked lint, capture enrichment (auto-filling `reasoning.tested` from transcripts — the one genuinely unfinished plan item), and a retrieval-quality eval to test whether the offline embedder default earns its keep; (2) *proving it elsewhere* — dogfooding on a real external project, the PR-comment recipe, a second capture adapter; (3) *surfaces gated on proven need* — Electron wrapper, shared-index server, hosted service, each with your previously-approved decisions starred so they don't get re-litigated; (4) *the v2 ideas* — with the **semantic drift detector** flagged as the strongest candidate for the next novel feature, since it turns the ledger from memory into an active guarantee.

**`CLAUDE.md`** is the collaboration distilled: the nine hard rules (each one earned — real git only, non-minting reads, hooks never break commits, JSONL writes, honest degradation, package boundaries, your RAM rule, the scoped API key, the humans-get-the-page/agents-get-JSON split), the milestone-agent pattern with independent re-verification before every commit, the specific process lessons (explicit-path staging, unpiped gate commands, checkpointed long runs — all three learned from real slips), your working style, and the Windows quirks. Any future Claude Code session in this repo loads it automatically — and it points them at `git for-ai ask` before re-deriving old decisions, which is rather the point of the whole thing.

Honest answer: you don't need it *today* — it's on the roadmap as the standard maturity step, not an urgent one. Here's the actual calculus:

**What you have now**: the CLI works on this machine only because `npm link` wired a symlink from your global npm into `packages/cli`. That's fragile in specific ways — it breaks if `node_modules` gets wiped, it requires the full dev setup (clone, pnpm, build) to reproduce, and it exists on exactly one machine.

**What publishing would buy, in order of relevance to you:**

1. **Using git-for-ai on your other machines and projects.** The moment you want the intent layer on a second computer — or just want a laptop to run `git for-ai review` against a synced repo — `npm install -g git-for-ai` is the difference between thirty seconds and reproducing the dev environment. This is the first real trigger.
2. **Anyone else using it.** Your stated goal from day one was "personal tool first, clean enough to open-source later." Publishing *is* the open-sourcing moment for the tool half (the repo going public is the other half). No second user, no need yet.
3. **Small correctness details** that only matter at publish time and are cheap to get right early: the workspace-internal packages (`core`, `schemas`, `review-ui`) need bundling or publishing alongside; the engines floor needs declaring (`node:sqlite` needs Node ≥22.5); and the `claude mcp add git-for-ai -- git-for-ai mcp` snippet in the README quietly assumes the binary is on PATH — true for anyone via publish, true only via link today.

**What it does *not* involve**: your data. The package is just the tool; ledgers, sessions, and indexes stay in each repo. No telemetry, no service.

**One wrinkle worth knowing before ever pressing the button**: the public npm name `git-for-ai` may collide or sit near existing projects (`git-ai` exists in the landscape research), so name availability needs a check — and publishing to the public registry is a one-way door reputationally (unpublishing is restricted). A middle path exists if you only want machine no. 2: installing straight from the GitHub repo, or a private registry, without going public.

So my recommendation stands as written in the roadmap tier but with the gate made explicit: **do nothing until you have a second machine or a first outside user** — `npm link` is entirely adequate for one dev box. When either trigger arrives, it's roughly a day of work (bundling decision, engines field, name check, dry-run install on a clean machine). Want me to demote it in the roadmap to make that gating explicit?
Three solid threads there. Before writing the plan, let me *test* the branching/merging question empirically rather than reason from memory — it takes two minutes with the real tool:

body.text: Squash-merge is the confirmed weak spot, exactly as your instinct suggested. Full findings in a moment — writing the plan now with the evidence baked in:

attributes.command:
cd C:/src/git-for-ai && git add architecture/DESKTOP.md architecture/ROADMAP.md && git commit -q -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
Add DESKTOP.md: desktop app plan grounded in tested branch/merge behavior

Owner direction: explore the desktop app next; a useful one must carry
git-client elements, which forced the branch/merge question - answered
empirically before designing. Verified working: branch commits, no-ff
merges (merge commit gets its own identity, merged commits keep
theirs), everything SHA-anchored and branch-agnostic. Confirmed gaps:
G1 merge --squash mints an UNLINKED squash change and leaves the
source branch's changes on commits that become unreachable after
branch delete (fix scoped: SQUASH_MSG detection in internal-hook
post-commit folds like the post-rewrite path, plus a doctor
unreachable-heads audit); G2 the index is single-rev (display it,
one-click reindex; multi-rev is v2); G3 change-map divergence across
machines still lacks a 3-way driver. Plus a discovered design rule:
metadata refs must be filtered from any all-branches view.

The app: a repository intelligence app, NOT a git client replica in
v1 (no staging/commit) - repo picker, branch-scoped views, diff
viewer with intent beside it, and a token-gated actions panel
(sync/reindex/annotate/repair), as an Electron shell around the same
server+SPA the browser uses. Build order: G1 fix -> read-only API
groundwork (rev/branches/diff, browser benefits immediately) -> UI
panes -> Electron shell -> packaging.

ROADMAP updated: desktop promoted to active; npm publish gated on a
second machine/user, with the owner's naming decision recorded
(git-for-ai is the internal name only; public name TBD).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
)" && git push origin main "+refs/notes/git-for-ai/*:refs/notes/git-for-ai/*" "+refs/git-for-ai/*:refs/git-for-ai/*" 2>&1 | tail -3
